title: 2026 Made Bike Show Picks 07: Breadwinner, Donkelope, MMFG, Mosaic, Pine, Seeker, Singular – Paul Kalifatidi
content:
Team Radavist is on the ground at the 2026 Made Bike Show, documenting a selection of bikes. Paul perused the available offerings and selected bikes from Breadwinner, Donkelope, MMFG, Mosaic, Pine, Seeker, and Singular. Read on for a jam-packed gallery full of details in our Picks 07 post!

The Radavist thanks Shimano for sponsoring our Made Bike Show coverage and our independent Reportage!

Breadwinner B-Road Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Tony Pereira helped found Breadwinner Cycles in 2013. Since then, the Portland-based framebuilder has existed in a variety of sizes. Now, it’s just Tony. He brought this lovely turquoise and pink bike with matching bags from Jack’s Sacks. I heard multiple “oh it’s so cute” comments from showgoers.

I’ve seen lots of Breadwinner bikes over the years, and I’ve always appreciated their timeless design. There is nothing cutting-edge. There are no fads. They are simply quality bicycles. Tony even asked me if he should be making 32″ wheeled bikes. I told him that I thought they were neat for the right people, but in the end, they are just bikes, and a Breadwinner is a bicycle.

Tony, it was great to finally meet you!

@BreadWinnerCycles

Donkelope Big Green Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Greg Heath, the builder of Donkelope Bikes, is a local legend in Bellingham, Washington. Frankly, Kyber, his lovable canine companion, might actually steal the show. Kyber isn’t in these photos because he was too busy chasing the tail of his cat friend, who also came down from Bellingham for the show.

Greg and I spent all of our time chatting, so much so that I completely forgot to photograph the bike that he made for a friend. I have plenty of photos of Greg with the bike, so you’re going to have to enjoy those. Greg’s customer is a long-time friend of his, a friend who is quite tall. It was cool to see such a tall bike at this show that didn’t feature 32″ tires, a theme that presented itself in just about every booth at Made.

Greg is the real deal on a BMX and dirt jumper. Every time I see him, he has some kind of update on a local jump line, legislative drama when it comes to a skate park, or he has recently crashed trying some maneuver I am incapable of and warns me not to hug him where his ribs are broken. Greg, you walk the walk. Thanks for hanging!

@Donkelope

Montenegro MFG Acid Flame Full Suspension MTB – Paul Kalifatidi

This full suspension bike caught my eye. It was in the Wolf Tooth Builder’s Lounge where lots of bikes were on display. The acid green flames and matching rear triangle give it some real pop, much like how I imagine the bike must ride.

Montenegro MFG is from Los Angeles and built by Hernan Montenegro. A metal bike is actually a bit of an outlier in Hernan’s framebuilding story; he mostly focuses on custom carbon fiber bicycles, components, and repair. This bike is a steel full-suspension mountain bike that uses a single-pivot suspension design. Interestingly, there is what appears to be a 3D-printed brace connecting the rear triangle under the shock mount. I’m curious if this piece can be modified to change the stiffness of the frame.

I dig this mountain bike and hope that Hernan does more bikes like it.

@Montenegro_MFG

Mosaic GT-1 i55 Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Mosaic Bikes always bring a stunning fleet of bikes from Boulder, CO, to Portland for Made. This year was no different, and they brought some new optional finishes too. I chatted with founder and framebuilder Aaron Barcheck about this lovely green bike.

Once you learn Mosaic’s naming scheme, it’s easy to peruse their models and understand what they are. GT indicates that this is a gravel bike, 1 denotes that it is Mosaic’s highest-end double-butted tubeset, and i55 stands for integrated routing and 55 mm of tire clearance. For another example, a GT-2 is a straight-gauge tubeset gravel bike.

I immediately noticed the chainstay yoke and asked Aaron if it was new, as I had never seen one like it on a Mosaic. Turns out, this is the first time that Mosaic has ever used a 3D-printed component in a frame. It’s subtle and well done. Speaking of well done, check out the welds on the dropouts: stacks of dimes.

Aaron, thanks for chatting and showing me your stunning work!

@MosaicCycles

Pine Cycles FRST – Paul Kalifatidi

If you haven’t been keeping track, this is the third green bike in a row. I like a green bike and really want one finished in river rock green. Kevin of PINE Cycles was at the show to show off his green bike and a variety of other things he has been working on.

This FRST uses the new Frequency Fork from Slug and features a fully integrated cockpit that uses a prototype Thomson system that Kevin has been helping design. Kevin also helped Mosaic with their new line of Zero Components, forks and other carbon bits for framebuilders and OEMs alike. He helped design the Enve adventure fork, so you’re probably already familiar with his work. Kevin, please leave some design work for the rest of us!

The FRST is a sweet bike. To attempt to put a label on it, I’d call it a wide-tire gravel bike that splits the difference between an aggressive-position race bike and an upright endurance machine. It’s the perfect PNW bike where we tend not to have really high-speed riding unless you’re descending, where control and capability matter far more than aerodynamic efficiency. Kevin also has some new stuff in the works at PINE and showed off these minimalist carbon rims. In an industry filled with aggressively decaled hoops, these stand out for their simplicity. Keep your eyes peeled on PINE if you’re into these.

Kevin, thanks for talking bikes with me. I hope to see more of your design work out there and look forward to seeing you in Seattle sooner rather than later!

@PineCycles

Seeker Titanium Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

If you’re in the market for a sleek, simple, well-made, and thoughtfully designed titanium gravel bike, your seeking can end with a Seeker. You can’t have this one, though; this is the first bike that Chris McGovern has made for himself in six years.

Chris told me that he has finally landed on what he thinks a Seeker should look like. He’s made a lot of bikes over the years, and this is his favorite phenotype. There are numerous features that make this bike ride as good as it looks. Not only is the monostay that splits into the seatstays easier to make and has the aesthetic he likes, but joining the seat tube far below the top tube adds a lot of frame compliance. It helps the seatpost deflect more than if the tubes all met in the same place. He has also spent a lot of time designing the 3D-printed yoke. He had another bike on display, a 32er where clearance is even harder to find, and that one had a yoke with both driveside and non-driveside printed pieces.

Chris is also afflicted with the same disease as me: a Toyota. Some say that Toyotas are reliable, but his 3rd gen 4Runner is in the shop and I have enough trauma with my Prado that I accidentally became a journalist. Regardless, I think this appreciation for practical and capable vehicles bleeds into his bike design. There is nothing superfluous, decor is minimal, and the design is pragmatic.

Chris, I wish you equal compression on all cylinders and happy trails!

@SeekerADV

Singular Swift – Paul Kalifatidi

We’ll end my coverage of the bikes at Made with this beautiful Singular Swift that was painted by Portland-based artist Chet Malinow. Like most people who pay attention to this corner of the greater bike industry, I was aware of Singular Cycles but wasn’t fully vested in my knowledge of the brand until I wrote one of our radar posts about the new Peregrine. I appreciated the attention to detail when it came to their bikes, and the evolution of the brand: small refinements instead of sweeping changes and thoughtful component selection are what I noticed most.

This bike was displayed at the Biciclista booth, where it was showcasing some Ingrid Components and generally welcoming people with its warm orange vibe. I’m not actually sure if there was a more orange bike at the show. It also might have been the only bike to have an 11-speed SRAM GX drivetrain, adding to the general humility exhibited by a Singular.

I’m happy to conclude my bike galleries with this one. I think it is the kind of bike that is missing from my quiver, if you can call two and a half bikes a quiver. It seems like a joy to ride slow, look around, and appreciate the world. That is what we need a lot more of from a lot more people. Singular, thanks for leaving me with these pleasant thoughts.

@SingularCycles

 

Well, that’s a wrap for our second 2026 Made Bike Show gallery. Which bike is your favorite, and what would you like to see us document from the show?
